claims.text: The starting material is a precursor noble-metal high-entropy alloy or a partially alloyed multi-noble-metal structure.
Multi-step electrochemical dealloying can produce noble-metal-based HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
A machine-learning model can optimize the parameter sets used for multi-step electrochemical dealloying.
The dealloying process will use controlled electrolyte compositions, regulated potential profiles, and regulated temperatures.
The process will form an interconnected three-dimensional porous nanoframework.
The resulting porous nanoframework will preserve the precursor's high-entropy composition.
Optimized dealloying conditions selectively remove less-noble constituents.
Selective dealloying can maintain a uniform distribution of the retained noble metals.
Selective removal of less-noble constituents while retaining noble metals forms a stable three-dimensional architecture.
The resulting nanostructure provides increased numbers of active catalytic sites.
Machine-learning-optimized dealloying will yield more uniform porosity than fixed-parameter dealloying.
Machine-learning-optimized dealloying will yield greater elemental fidelity than fixed-parameter dealloying.
The greater structural and compositional control will improve catalytic performance.
Conventional one-step or non-optimized dealloying generally produces irregular and less compositionally controlled porous structures.
The proposed method applies to noble-metal HEAs containing five or more noble-metal elements.
Scalability and reproducibility at substantially different system sizes or compositions remain untested.
The precise dealloying parameter values and magnitude of performance improvement are not yet defined.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in structural uniformity, composition fidelity, and catalytic performance relative to fixed-parameter controls would falsify the hypothesis.
